title: A general, detail-free allocation compiler for private-information economies

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reusable system that turns an allocation objective, a description of participants’ private information, and explicit constraints into a mechanism: rules for reporting information, assigning resources and making payments. Its output would include proved guarantees about incentives, participation, budget requirements and allocation performance. The ambition is to make mechanism design programmable across a specified broad class of economies, while reducing dependence on the designer’s knowledge of precise probability distributions over participants’ information.

Proposed scope includes economies with complements, where combinations of goods matter; interdependent values, where one participant’s information affects another’s valuation; dynamics, where information and decisions unfold over time; and thin markets with few potential trading partners. These are target domains, not capabilities demonstrated by the supplied evidence. “General” would require explicit admissible domains and guarantees appropriate to each; it would not mean an unrestricted solution for arbitrary economies. “Detail-free” is used here operationally to mean limited dependence on fine details of priors. The supplied material does not substantiate the original attribution of that terminology to Wilson.

The motivating distinction is between knowing that a good mechanism exists for a particular statistical model and having a practical way to construct one with little prior information. The supplied bilateral-trade paper describes second-best mechanisms as potentially complex and sensitive to precise priors. A compiler would have to bridge this gap between an implicitly defined optimum and an implementable allocation rule; the paper’s performance theorem does not itself provide that bridge.

significance.text: Conditional significance: a sufficiently broad, practical compiler could make guaranteed mechanism construction reusable across new private-information allocation problems. Its direct contribution would be a systematic way to produce rules and explicit performance guarantees within demonstrated domains. The analogy to a general-purpose computer concerns making a specialized intellectual activity programmable; it is an impact judgment, not evidence that every allocation problem admits an efficient or computationally tractable solution.

The technical motivation is substantial: the supplied paper describes the second-best bilateral-trade mechanism as implicitly defined, potentially highly complex and dependent on exact priors. A practical system that retained useful guarantees with weaker informational requirements would address an obstacle already visible in a market with only one buyer and one seller.

Conditional downstream possibilities include reducing repeated custom design work and extending reliable allocation methods to unfamiliar markets. Near-efficient outcomes and faster deployment would require more than an unspecified approximation guarantee: the approximation factors must be strong, computation tractable, inputs reliable and implementation successful. The supplied evidence does not establish a decade-long baseline for custom design, that every historical success was bespoke, or the scale of any resulting time savings.

The breakthrough would operate within impossibility constraints or explicitly change their assumptions. Exact efficiency remains excluded under the classical Myerson–Satterthwaite conditions. Likewise, obtaining more than half of first-best surplus in selected thin markets would be compatible with the cited paper’s one-half worst-case result. A claim to exceed that uniform guarantee would need to identify a restricted domain or a changed information, incentive, participation or budget assumption and demonstrate why the original bound no longer applies.

missing_breakthrough.text: The proposed missing capability is an end-to-end method that accepts a formally specified economy and returns a usable mechanism together with verifiable guarantees, without requiring precise prior distributions wherever the promised robustness applies. The supplied evidence motivates this goal through prior sensitivity and complexity in bilateral trade. It does not establish the present-day absence of such technology throughout all the richer domains proposed here.

A foundational barrier is that desirable properties can be mutually incompatible. Under the classical Myerson–Satterthwaite distributional and informational assumptions, Bayesian incentive compatibility, individual rationality and budget balance preclude ex post efficient bilateral trade. Bayesian incentive compatibility concerns truthful reporting in expectation over others’ information; individual rationality concerns participants’ willingness to take part. The impossibility must not be read as applying to every possible pair of valuation distributions. A compiler must identify which guarantees are feasible under its declared assumptions and expose unavoidable tradeoffs.

A separate barrier is the gap between an optimal mechanism with known priors and a simple mechanism that can be deployed with limited knowledge. The cited model assumes independent buyer and seller valuations and that the designer knows their distributions. Its second-best benchmark therefore does not establish a detail-free construction. Preserving useful surplus guarantees while reducing information requirements, controlling computational complexity and producing rules participants can actually use remains the central engineering ambition.

Research synthesis: extending this ambition to the proposed richer domains would require handling interactions among allocations when goods are complements, information dependence when values are interdependent, and commitments and incentives across time in dynamic settings. Thin markets also offer fewer opportunities to offset one participant’s informational advantage through competition. These are concrete dimensions the compiler would need to address, but the supplied source does not provide general results covering them. A further challenge is measuring performance against an estimated first-best benchmark when the relevant information is itself private.

current_state.text: Zhengyang Liu, Ying Qin, Zeyu Ren and Zihe Wang’s “Second-Best Bilateral Trade is 1/2 Efficient” was first submitted to arXiv on 2 June 2026 and revised on 5 July 2026. The supplied review identifies it as an arXiv preprint. The available material does not independently establish whether a peer-reviewed version exists, so the original categorical description “not peer-reviewed” is not retained.

The paper reports a tight one-half worst-case guarantee for expected gains from trade in its model of one buyer, one seller and one indivisible good with independent private values. Subject to Bayesian incentive compatibility, interim individual rationality and strong or weak budget balance, the second-best achieves at least half of first-best expected gains from trade. Interim individual rationality evaluates participation conditional on a participant’s own information and in expectation over the other participant’s information. Strong budget balance requires transfers to balance exactly; weak budget balance allows a surplus but no deficit.

First-best here is the expected surplus available from efficient trade without the same incentive and participation restrictions; second-best is the best expected surplus attainable under the model’s mechanism constraints. Tightness means there are examples whose second-best-to-first-best ratios approach one half. It does not mean every market loses half its surplus, that a ratio of exactly one half must be attained by a particular example, or that no individual market can perform better. The paper also states that no mechanism satisfying the relevant constraints can guarantee a uniformly higher worst-case ratio across its model class.

The introduction reports approximately 0.317 as an earlier best-known lower guarantee for a simple mechanism. That comparison must preserve the distinction between a restricted simple mechanism and the unrestricted second-best benchmark: the one-half theorem does not establish that an equally simple, prior-robust mechanism attains the same guarantee. These are theoretical approximation results in a restricted domain, not evidence of a deployed compiler for complements, interdependent values or dynamic economies.

The supplied review could assess the identified landing page, theorem statements and portions of the paper, but the retained PDF extraction stops mid-proof on page 47. Consequently, the complete proof, including the full tightness argument, was not available for inspection in that review. The landing-page extraction is complete as a landing page, not as a full paper. This access limitation does not show that the reported result is false; it limits the depth of verification supported by the supplied record.

The available record does not establish the broader field’s deployment history or whether a compiler meeting this proposal’s scope remained unavailable on 1 November 2026. The supplied freshness search record is empty. The dated July 2026 result remains relevant, but it cannot support an exhaustive current-field conclusion. Similarly, the research’s general references to successful special-case market design and other restricted-domain approximation results are not accompanied here by sources sufficient to document their breadth.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evaluation criteria: define the compiler’s admissible economies, required inputs, permitted prior information, incentive conditions, participation conditions and budget rule before testing. Specify target approximation factors and computational requirements, including the scale of problems it is intended to handle. State precisely what robustness to fine prior details means and which changes in distributions or information the guarantee covers. These would be proposed assessment requirements, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Define admissible economies, performance targets and prior-robustness guarantees before testing

completion_criteria.text: Proposed theoretical demonstration: on a new allocation problem outside families already engineered in the field, the compiler should produce a mechanism and a published, checkable approximation guarantee that respects applicable impossibility bounds. Its claims should distinguish best-possible constrained performance from the performance of the actual generated mechanism. If a claimed improvement depends on relaxing classical assumptions, those changes and their practical costs should be explicit.
completion_criteria.label: Generate mechanisms with checkable approximation guarantees for new allocation problems

completion_criteria.text: Proposed deployment demonstration: the generated mechanism should attain a pre-registered fraction of estimated first-best surplus without a subsidy and without requiring the designer to know the fine prior. The target fraction must be selected and justified in advance rather than inferred after observing outcomes. Evaluation should report uncertainty in the first-best estimate, whether incentive and participation conditions were met, computational costs, implementation difficulties and the boundaries within which the result held.
completion_criteria.label: Attain pre-registered first-best surplus fraction without subsidy or fine-prior knowledge

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and breadth requirements: release sufficient specifications, implementation details, proof materials and evaluation procedures for independent teams to reproduce the construction and assess its guarantees. Demonstrations across substantially different domains would be needed to support broad applicability. One unfamiliar application would establish progress; another spectrum auction or school-choice refinement alone would not satisfy this proposal’s novelty criterion. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth, not literal universality, and unsuccessful or unsupported domains should remain visible.
completion_criteria.label: Enable independent reproduction and demonstrate breadth across substantially different domains

related_concepts.text: Roster-based scope interpretation: ECO-05, “Approximately efficient voluntary provision of global public goods,” is the closest stated neighbor. Both involve allocation with incentives and voluntary participation. ECO-09 concerns reusable mechanism construction across private-information economies; ECO-05 focuses on global public-good provision. Public-good mechanisms could be applications of a sufficiently capable compiler, but that possibility does not merge the concepts. The proposed boundary follows the supplied titles and research; ECO-05’s full definition was not supplied.

Roster-based scope interpretation: ECO-03, “A predictive and welfare-coherent theory of boundedly rational choice,” concerns how people choose, whereas ECO-09 concerns designing allocation rules given an explicit behavioral model. Better models of choice could improve a compiler’s assumptions, but a guarantee of Bayesian incentive compatibility would not by itself establish performance under bounded rationality. ECO-04, “An interpersonally comparable, preference-respecting measure of welfare,” concerns what welfare means and how it can be compared. A compiler might optimize a supplied welfare objective without resolving that measurement problem.

Roster-based scope interpretation: ECO-01, “Empirically valid aggregate market laws beyond the Sonnenschein–Mantel–Debreu barrier,” concerns aggregate market regularities; ECO-09 concerns constructing rules for particular allocation environments. ECO-02, “Prospective transport of causal policy effects across populations,” concerns whether effects carry across populations. That could matter when transferring evidence about a mechanism between settings, but a formal mechanism guarantee under stated assumptions does not itself establish empirical transportability.

Roster-based scope interpretation: ECO-06, “Household-scale markets for national, occupational, and housing income risk,” and ECO-10, “Liquidity and credit without run-prone debt,” describe possible financial applications or institutional goals. An allocation compiler could potentially help design contracts or participation rules within such systems. It would not by itself create viable household risk markets or establish that a credit system avoids runs; those innovations retain their own requirements.

Roster-based scope interpretation: ECO-07, “A verified, manipulable law of sustained productivity growth,” and ECO-08, “Structural counterfactuals for macroeconomic regimes,” concern growth and macroeconomic prediction. Improved allocation could conditionally contribute to productivity, and macroeconomic models could inform an allocation objective. Mechanism construction would nevertheless establish neither a law of sustained growth nor reliable structural counterfactuals across regimes.

Disciplinary synthesis: ECO-09 lies at the intersection of economics and algorithmic mechanism design, with substantial computer-science requirements for computation, representation and verification. Its distinctive target is the combination of reusable construction, explicit guarantees, limited reliance on precise priors and demonstrated practical breadth. A result in any one of these areas would be a component of the proposed innovation, rather than evidence that the complete compiler has been achieved.

unresolved_issues: Whether a system meeting the proposed broad compiler specification existed as of 1 November 2026 is not established by the supplied record.
The complete retained proof is unavailable because the PDF extraction ends mid-proof on page 47; full independent verification of the lower guarantee and tightness remains outside this record.
Whether a peer-reviewed version of the cited preprint exists is unresolved.
The original attribution of “detail-free” to Wilson is not documented by the supplied source.
The admissible rich domains, precise prior-information requirements, robustness definition, computational limits and useful approximation targets remain to be specified.
Any relaxation intended to improve on a classical worst-case guarantee must identify exactly which assumptions change and whether the change is practically defensible.
Reliable estimation of first-best surplus in a deployment, including uncertainty caused by private information, remains an evaluation problem.
The full definitions of the related roster concepts were not supplied; their overlap and boundaries, especially with ECO-05, remain provisional.

brief.title: Software that designs rules for sharing resources
possible: People organising markets could describe what they want to achieve, what participants know privately and what rules must hold. Software would turn that description into rules for reporting information, assigning resources and making payments, with proofs of what those rules guarantee.

The same system could serve very different markets without needing precise predictions of participants’ private values. Its intended reach includes goods that are valuable together, decisions that unfold over time and markets with few trading partners.
why: Market designers could reuse a systematic construction process instead of repeatedly solving unfamiliar problems from scratch. They would get explicit guarantees about honest reporting, willingness to participate, funding needs and how much value the rules preserve.

sources.who: Zhengyang Liu, Ying Qin, Zeyu Ren and Zihe Wang
sources.showed: Their preprint proves that the best trading rules under their honesty, participation and budget conditions preserve at least half the ideal gain from trade when buyer and seller values are independent. That worst-case guarantee cannot be improved across the model.
sources.quote:
Finally, we prove tightness by constructing a family of
distributions whose second-best-to-first-best ratio converges to1/2.
sources.cited_for: It establishes a performance limit for trade between a buyer and a seller.
sources.not_established: It does not deliver a practical system that constructs rules without precise knowledge of value distributions.

sources.who: Roger B. Myerson and Mark A. Satterthwaite
sources.showed: They characterised trading rules that reward honest reporting and voluntary participation. Under their assumptions, such rules cannot always realise every beneficial trade without outside funding.
sources.quote:
We characterize the set of allocation mechanisms that are Bayesian 
incentive compatible and individually rational, and show the general impossibility 
of ex post efficient mechanisms without outside subsidies.
sources.cited_for: It identifies tradeoffs that any rule-generating system must respect.
sources.not_established: It does not provide a reusable construction system across the proposed range of markets.

sources.who: Zi Yang Kang, Francisco Pernice and Jan Vondrák
sources.showed: They proved that setting a price from a sample preserves a guaranteed share of total value when buyer and seller values follow the same distribution. Total value includes the seller’s value if no trade occurs.
sources.quote:
With just one prior sample from the common distribution, we s how that a 3 /4-approximation to welfare is
achievable.
sources.cited_for: It shows that useful trading guarantees can require little information about private values.
sources.not_established: Its total-value guarantee does not establish the same guarantee for gains from trade or for broader markets.

sources.showed: They built an efficient algorithm for choosing optimal rules in repeated interactions with a strategic participant when the decision horizon is fixed. They also proved computational limits for longer horizons.
sources.quote:
We give an efﬁcient algorithm for computing optimal mechanisms, with or without
payments, under different individual-rationality constraints, when the time horizon
is constant.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates automated rule construction for decisions that unfold over time.
sources.not_established: It does not establish practical construction across long horizons, many participants and limited distributional knowledge.

sources.who: Maria-Florina Balcan, Tuomas Sandholm and Ellen Vitercik
sources.showed: They established how much sample data specified families of auctions need for revenue measured on samples to predict expected revenue under the unknown distribution of bidders’ values.
sources.quote:
We present tight sample complexity guarantees over an extensive
hierarchy of expressive CA families.
sources.cited_for: It supports learning auction rules from examples rather than knowing the full distribution of private values.
sources.not_established: Reliable revenue estimates within auction families do not establish a general system with all the proposed guarantees.

shown: Liu and colleagues’ preprint establishes a sharp limit in a simple trading market: the best rules satisfying their conditions retain at least half the ideal gain from trade. That gain is the buyer’s value minus the seller’s value when trade occurs.

Working construction methods cover narrower settings. Zhang and Conitzer automate rules for repeated interactions over a fixed horizon. Kang and colleagues prove guarantees with limited information, while Balcan and colleagues establish how sample data can support auction design.
missing: A reusable system must turn a market description into usable rules with checkable guarantees and limited dependence on precise value distributions.
The system must handle goods valued together, values affected by others’ information, decisions over time and few trading partners.
Practical demonstrations must establish manageable computation, participant usability and reliable estimates of the ideal value available.

milestones.label: A defined scope and testable guarantees
milestones.explanation: The system’s market scope, inputs, information needs, honesty and participation conditions, budget rules, performance targets and computing limits would have to be fixed before testing. This makes its promises assessable.

milestones.label: Generated rules with checkable guarantees for unfamiliar problems
milestones.explanation: For an unfamiliar allocation problem, the system would have to generate rules with a checkable performance guarantee that respects applicable limits. This connects a theoretical possibility to rules the system actually produces.

milestones.label: A deployment meets its declared value target without subsidy
milestones.explanation: A deployment would have to meet a target share of estimated ideal gains chosen in advance, without subsidy or precise distributional knowledge. Uncertainty and operating costs would establish how meaningful that success is.

milestones.label: Independent reproduction across substantially different markets
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce the construction and assess its guarantees across substantially different markets using released methods and materials. This would establish demonstrated breadth and reproducibility.

uncertain: Which markets admit useful guarantees with limited knowledge of private-value distributions and manageable computation?
How reliably can ideal gains be estimated when the information needed to calculate them is private?
Would changes to assumptions that permit stronger guarantees remain defensible in practice?

page.title: Prior-robust automated mechanism design
page.definition: A reusable program converts an economy’s objective, constraints and limited information about participants’ private values into allocation and payment rules with proved guarantees. One synthesis method covers specified domains with goods valued jointly, values affected by others’ information, decisions over time and few traders.

goal.need: GAO’s fiscal year 2012 procurement data document auctions with only one vendor. Even with one buyer and one seller, Liu et al.’s 2026 arXiv preprint reports a tight 1/2 worst-case ratio of attainable expected gains from trade to efficient gains, under independent private values, Bayesian incentive compatibility, interim participation and budget balance. Mechanism construction must accommodate limited competition, incomplete distributional knowledge and incompatible objectives.

completion.title: One executable system synthesizes mechanisms with proved guarantees under distributional uncertainty.
completion.criterion: For every feasible specification in its declared finite static and dynamic domains, one program generates executable allocation and payment rules meeting the input’s numerical performance target and incentive, participation and budget constraints for every distribution in a specified non-singleton uncertainty set. Supported domains include complementary goods, interdependent values and few traders. Sample-derived uncertainty sets have a stated coverage probability. Correctness and computational bounds apply throughout the admitted domains, and the implementation realizes the proved construction.
completion.set_by: Atlas provisional completion criterion, combining published automated-design and robustness objectives; no external combined test located.
completion.basis: Searches for an automated mechanism design roadmap, standard, prize rule, shared benchmark and robust-synthesis target located no combined completion test. Sandholm specifies instance-specific construction; SEI requests convergence to a chosen quality goal; Albert et al. define constraints over uncertain distributions. Numerical performance targets therefore remain inputs rather than a field-wide approximation factor. Feasible specifications must respect bilateral-trade impossibility.

milestones.title: An algorithm computes an optimal truthful randomized mechanism for 2 agents in polynomial time.
milestones.criterion: For 2 agents with explicitly represented finite type and outcome sets, known independent type distributions and no side payments, compute a randomized direct mechanism maximizing the supplied expected objective subject to dominant-strategy truthfulness. The objective must be polynomially computable. Runtime is polynomial in the explicit input size. Conitzer and Sandholm established this result in Theorem 3; Theorem 4 establishes the corresponding Bayes–Nash result.
milestones.set_by: Finite automated mechanism design optimization convention, formalized by Conitzer and Sandholm in Complexity of Mechanism Design, Theorems 3–4.
milestones.threshold_quote: is solvable in polynomial time by linear programming, for any (polynomially computable) objective function.

milestones.title: Mixed-bundling auction revenues generalize within ε from samples with probability at least 1−δ.
milestones.criterion: For the paper’s class of n-bidder, m-item mixed-bundling auctions, obtain simultaneous absolute error at most ε between sample-average and expected revenue, with probability at least 1−δ over independent valuation-profile samples. If revenue is bounded by U, Theorem 4 gives sufficient sample size N = O((U/ε)²[log(U/ε) + log(1/δ)]). Definition 1 specifies the uniform guarantee. Balcan, Sandholm and Vitercik proved this in 2016.
milestones.set_by: Statistical uniform-convergence convention applied to automated mechanism design by Balcan, Sandholm and Vitercik, Definition 1 and Theorem 4.
milestones.threshold_quote: We do achieve polynomial sample complexity upper bounds for the important classes of mixed bundling auctions

milestones.title: An algorithm computes an optimal dynamic mechanism in polynomial time when the horizon is fixed.
milestones.criterion: For a principal interacting with one strategic agent over a constant finite horizon, compute a mechanism maximizing the principal’s expected utility subject to incentive compatibility and the selected participation and payment restrictions. The state and action sets are finite and the environment’s probabilities are inputs. Theorem 2 gives runtime polynomial in |S|^T, |A|^T and parameter encoding length, where T is the horizon. Zhang and Conitzer proved the result in 2021.
milestones.set_by: Automated dynamic mechanism design optimization problem defined by Zhang and Conitzer, Theorem 2; the published threshold concerns one strategic agent.
milestones.threshold_quote: when the time horizon is fixed, there is a polynomial-time algorithm for computing optimal mechanisms

milestones.title: A synthesis algorithm maximizes a mechanism’s logical specification in two decidable classes.
milestones.criterion: Given a Quantitative Strategy Logic specification and a finite set of proposition values, construct a weighted concurrent game structure—a formal model of strategic interaction—with the greatest attainable specification value. Algorithm 1 supplies this construction for bounded-action systems and turn-based systems. Mittelmann et al. established the synthesis result in 2022 and gave auction specifications as examples. The result does not supply polynomial runtime.
milestones.set_by: Logical synthesis convention instantiated by Mittelmann et al., Automated Synthesis of Mechanisms, Theorems 2–3 and Algorithm 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: it works in the case of bounded actions and the case of turn-based systems.

milestones.title: An algorithm computes an optimal robust mechanism in polynomial time for finite bidder and signal types.
milestones.criterion: For one bidder with a finite valuation type and a correlated, externally verifiable finite signal, maximize revenue under the estimated joint distribution while enforcing Bayesian truthfulness and interim participation for every conditional distribution in the specified uncertainty sets. Each conditional set must be a convex polyhedron with polynomially many defining inequalities. Corollary 4 proves polynomial computation within the class of mechanisms depending on the reported type and observed signal.
milestones.set_by: Albert, Conitzer and Stone’s published robust-mechanism optimization problem, Definition 10, Assumption 1 and Corollary 4; written for one bidder and an external signal.
milestones.threshold_quote: the optimal robust mechanism can be computed in time polynomial in the number of types of the bidder and external signal.

milestones.title: One constructive method meets stated guarantees across static and dynamic domains under prior uncertainty.
milestones.criterion: A single algorithm computes allocation and payment rules from objective and constraint specifications, with a proof that the input’s numerical performance, incentive, participation and budget conditions hold throughout a non-singleton uncertainty set. Its declared input classes include finite static and dynamic private-information economies admitting complementary goods, interdependent values and few traders. Correctness and computational bounds cover every admitted feasible input. This constructive result leaves executable implementation as the completion step.
milestones.set_by: Atlas provisional integration milestone; searches of published automated-design, robust-design and dynamic-synthesis criteria located no external test for this combined construction.

not_found: No roadmap, standard, prize rule or shared benchmark specifying completion of a prior-robust compiler across the stated domains was located.
No external criterion for a unified constructive algorithm immediately preceding executable integration was located.
No peer-reviewed version of Liu et al.’s 2026 bilateral-trade preprint was located.

results.finding: For 2 agents, an optimal dominant-strategy truthful randomized mechanism is computable in polynomial time.
results.detail: The linear program maximizes the expected objective for independently distributed types and a polynomially computable objective, without side payments.
results.quote:
Theorem 3 2-agent RANDOMIZED-
MECHANISM-DESIGN with dominant strategies
implementation as the solution concept is solvable
in polynomial time by linear programming, for any
(polynomially computable) objective function.

results.finding: Mixed-bundling auctions: a uniform ε-error guarantee follows for sufficiently many independent valuation samples.
results.detail: Theorem 3.9 and Lemma 3.19 imply a bound with sample complexity depending on n and m. The supplied text refers to a stronger specialized guarantee for mixed-bundling auctions, but does not state it or the milestone’s specified sample-size bound.
results.quote:
Mixed-bundling auctions [50] are MBARPs with no reserve prices. We provide a stronger,
specialized guarantee for this class in Appendix A.2.

results.detail: The result concerns a related dynamic game framework with a mediator and discusses payments, but does not establish the specified participation and payment restrictions or the stated |S|^T, |A|^T runtime bound.

results.finding: Algorithm 1 synthesizes an optimal weighted game structure in 2 classes; no empirical sample.
results.detail: The classes are bounded-action and turn-based systems, with a finite set of proposition values. The paper does not claim polynomial runtime.
results.quote:
This algorithm synthesizes
a wCGS that maximizes the satisfaction value of the given
SL[F ] specification, in all cases where the satisfiability prob-
lem for SL[F ] can be solved and a witness produced. In par-
ticular, it works in the case of bounded actions and the case
of turn-based systems.

results.finding: For one bidder, Corollary 4 proves polynomial-time computation in the numbers of bidder types and signal types.
results.detail: The result applies to mechanisms depending on the reported type and observed signal, with polyhedral conditional uncertainty sets. The source is a conference proceedings paper; the supplied text does not establish its review status.
results.quote:
Corollary 4. If P(ˆπ) satisﬁes Assumption 1, the optimal
robust mechanism can be computed in time polynomial in
the number of types of the bidder and external signal.

results.finding: For one bidder, an optimal robust mechanism is computable in polynomial time in the numbers of bidder and signal types.
results.detail: Conditional uncertainty sets must be convex polyhedra with polynomially many defining inequalities. The result is numbered Corollary 2 in this submitted manuscript, rather than Corollary 4.
results.quote: An optimal ϵ-robust mechanism can be computed in polynomial time.
